title: Container Security Basics
summary: The hygiene practices specific to containers, ahead of the deeper cloud IAM and security topics elsewhere in this area.

slides.markdown:
Container security starts long before deployment: it's decided by which base image you chose, whether it's been scanned, and how little privilege the running process actually needs.

Most real container breaches trace back to one of a small handful of avoidable choices — an unscanned base image, a container running as root, or a secret baked into a layer — not some exotic zero-day.

slides.subTitle: Base image choice is a security decision
slides.markdown:
Every layer you inherit from a base image is code you're trusting without having reviewed it yourself. A base image from an unknown publisher might bundle outdated packages, unnecessary tools that widen the attack surface, or worse, deliberately malicious code.

Prefer **official** or **verified publisher** images, prefer minimal bases (fewer packages means fewer potential vulnerabilities), and know exactly which base image and version every one of your production images is built from.

slides.subTitle: In the build pipeline
slides.markdown:
A scanner inspects an image's layers against a database of known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in OS packages and language dependencies, and flags anything matching a known issue with a severity rating. Running this as a **pipeline gate** — failing the build on a critical finding — catches problems before they ever reach a registry, let alone production.

Scanning once at build time isn't enough either: new CVEs are published constantly, so images already deployed should be re-scanned periodically against the growing vulnerability database.

slides.subTitle: Non-root, read-only filesystems, dropped capabilities
slides.markdown:
Three concrete levers shrink a container's blast radius if it's ever compromised: run as a **non-root** user so a compromised process can't act with root privileges; mount the root filesystem **read-only** (with explicit writable mounts only where genuinely needed) so an attacker can't persist changes; and **drop Linux capabilities** the process doesn't need (e.g. `NET_RAW`, `SYS_ADMIN`) rather than granting the full default set.

None of these require rewriting the application — they're configuration decisions applied at build or run time.

slides.sectionTitle: Secrets at runtime vs baked in
slides.markdown:
| | Baked into the image | Injected at runtime |
|---|---|---|
| Where it lives | Inside a layer — permanent, extractable by anyone with the image | In memory only, for the life of that one container |
| Rotation | Requires rebuilding and redeploying the image | Just update the secret store; running containers pick it up on next restart |
| Exposure | Anyone who pulls the image gets the secret | Only the running container (and whoever can exec into it) sees it |

**How to decide:** secrets should never be a build-time input — inject them at container start via environment variables from a secrets manager, or mounted files that aren't part of any image layer.

**Image signing** cryptographically attests that a specific image was produced by a specific, trusted build process and hasn't been tampered with since. A deployment pipeline can then be configured to **refuse to run unsigned images**, closing off a class of supply-chain attack where a compromised registry or a man-in-the-middle swaps in a malicious image with the same tag.

This is a briefly-mentioned but increasingly standard practice as supply-chain attacks on the software build process have become a real, recurring incident category.

slides.subTitle: Hardening a root-by-default container
slides.markdown:
Turning a container that runs as root by default into a hardened one:

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-slim
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --ingroup app app
USER app
```

```bash
docker run --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE myapp
```

The Dockerfile switches the process to an unprivileged user before it ever runs; the run flags make the filesystem read-only and drop every Linux capability except the one narrow permission (binding to a low port) the app actually needs.

**Wrong belief:** "It's a popular public image with lots of downloads, so it must be safe to run in production as-is."

**Why it's wrong:** popularity says nothing about whether the version you pulled has known, unpatched CVEs today — vulnerabilities are discovered continuously, and an image clean last month may not be now. It also doesn't protect against a maintainer account being compromised upstream.

**Correct model:** scan every image before it reaches production, pin to a specific patched version, and re-scan on a schedule so newly discovered CVEs in deployed images get caught.
